items.title: US inflation rises more than expected - here's what is happening with prices
items.summary: The pace of price rises increased to 3.7% in the year to September, driving by higher motor fuel costs.
items.content:
US inflation rose by more than expected in the year to September, according to official figures, in the final data release before the midterm elections next month.
The pace of price rises increased to 3.7%, up from 3.4% in the 12 months to August.
Inflation was above forecasts, driven by higher petrol prices, which have risen following disruption to Middle East energy supplies due to the US-Israel conflict with Iran.
The elections are being fought over cost-of-living pressures across the US.
Inflation is the rate at which the price of products or services increases over time.
For example, if a bottle of milk costs $1 but rises to $1.10 a year later, then annual inflation for bottled milk is 10%.
Officials from the Bureau of Labor Statistics measure inflation through the consumer price index (CPI).
It tracks the price changes of hundreds of day-to-day items including fresh food, gasoline and medical services to work out the overall level of inflation in the US economy.
The bureau updates this so-called basket of goods over time as peoples' spending and lifestyle habits change.
There are several factors that can cause inflation to rise.
If demand for a product outstrips its supply, that can lead to producers raising prices - the craze for Labubu dolls in recent years and the high resale prices are an example.
Higher incomes can also lead to higher demand, for example, which in turn pushes up prices.
Image caption, Supply and demand: Labubu dolls illustrate how inflation can rise
Supply can also affect inflation. If supply of a product is reduced, but demand remains constant, that can cause prices to rise. A good example of this is crude oil, which is used to make gasoline and diesel.
Before the US-Israel war with Iran began, it was trading at just over $70 a barrel, but when the conflict constricted crude supplies, the price quickly rose and is currently over $100.
Inflation has risen to 3.7% in the year to September, which is a higher-than-expected increase fuelled by petrol prices.
Vehicle fuel prices jumped by 34.2% over 12 months.
In September alone, they jumped by 9.1%, accounting for more than half of the increase in inflation, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.
Overall, energy inflation was up by 20.4% over the year as prices for fuel oil, energy services and electricity climbed. Fuel oil, used in home heating, was up 74.2% over the year.
Experts said the US Federal Reserve - which sets the country's interest rate - will be closely watching to see if energy costs begin to affect other areas of the economy, such as food prices, and drive inflation higher.
At the moment, food inflation remains subdued. It was flat over the month of September, and was 2.5% across the year.
Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, was 2.6%.
Will the inflation hike change Social Security payments?
Shortly after the latest inflation figure was released, the Social Security Administration announced that Social Security benefits including old age, survivors and disability insurance would rise by a similar amount - 3.6% - in 2027.
The administration said that the 3.6% rise will mean an average retirement benefit increase of $75 a month.
The cost-of-living adjustment will take effect in January for about 72 million people, while increased payments for the 7.2m receiving the supplemental security income will start on 31 December.
Since coming into office for the second time, President Donald Trump has introduced tariffs on most US trading partners around the world.
While most of the additional global levies were outlawed by the Supreme Court in February, the president immediately announced a new 10% global tariff to replace them.
Trump argued the tariffs would increase America's tax earnings, boost manufacturing and encourage people to buy US-made goods, but the higher import taxes have also had an impact on inflation, according to research from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.
Image caption, US President Donald Trump raised tariffs
Higher tariffs - which are levies that businesses pay on the goods they import - directly raise prices for US companies unless the overseas firms they are buying from lower prices to absorb some of the cost.
In response to the new tariffs, the New York Fed found exporters reduced prices very little, meaning US-based businesses ended up absorbing nearly 90% of the cost of the added tax.
Indirectly, higher tariffs also affected the prices of locally made goods, as many US producers rely on parts or materials from overseas.
Overall, the Fed found that every percentage point increase in average tariffs led to nearly a 0.25% price increase for consumer goods after one year.
While inflation is currently above where the US Federal Reserve would like - it has a target of 2% - it has been much higher in previous years.
During the Covid pandemic, issues such as supply chain disruption started pushing inflation up.
Additionally, in early 2022 when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, oil prices surged over $100 a barrel.
Both of these factors helped to drive inflation to a peak of about 9%.
It's important to note that if inflation is rising at a slower rate, that does not mean prices are going down - it simply means prices are rising at a slower pace.
A bit of inflation is considered good for an economy as the Federal Reserve's target rate illustrates.
Many central banks consider inflation of about 2% or a little higher to be stable, and at a level that doesn't impact people's purchasing decisions.
Much below that, people can delay spending if they expect price rises to slow further, or to fall. That can lead to businesses reducing wages, or reducing the number of workers to cope with lower demand.

items.title: Why is Starlink internet so important on the battlefield in Ukraine?
items.summary: It is the "backbone of military communications in Ukraine" that provides vital high-speed internet to forces across the country.
items.content:
Starlink satellites operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX provide high-speed internet - something modern war relies heavily on.
For Ukraine, it is vital for communications on the battlefield and effective drone warfare.
Using Starlink, Ukrainian drones can stay connected to operators over longer distances than conventional radio networks and are less vulnerable to jamming.
But on Tuesday night, Starlink suddenly and unexpectedly restricted the speed at which drones could fly while still maintaining internet connection . This disrupted some battlefield "missions", a top Ukrainian official said, and hampered Kyiv's ability to protect itself from incoming Russian attacks.
The restriction at 100mph (160km/h) meant that any drone travelling faster than that lost connection and was effectively useless.
"Starlink gives Ukraine the ability to see what's coming, to protect people," Kurt Volker, former US ambassador to Nato, told the BBC's Radio 4 Today programme. "If you cut that off, then more people are going to get killed - and that is a very cynical and callous decision to slow that down the way that has been done."
Connectivity had been restored by Wednesday evening.
The move has once again shown how Starlink can impact the conflict, which has been raging since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Image caption, Operators use the Starlink network to stay connected to weapons like drones, so they can see targets and where the drone is heading
Starlink is an internet network that uses satellites in low Earth orbit to provide connectivity, particularly in remote areas and battlefields.
It currently relies on more than 10,000 active satellites, making Starlink the world's largest satellite constellation.
It is owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX, and is the company's biggest revenue driver.
While Starlink is for civilian use, Starshield is its military-grade service, designed for use by the Pentagon.
Starshield relies on the Starlink network, but has greater security like enhanced encryption so that sensitive information can be transmitted without interception.
The US government has allowed Ukraine to use Starlink and Starshield in its defence against Russia. Musk cut Moscow's access to the service in February , giving Kyiv an advantage in the conflict.
Put simply, Starlink uses its thousands of satellites to ping high-speed internet back to almost every corner of the globe, using terminals on the ground that users can easily buy and set up themselves. As Musk said, they have two instructions: "point at sky, plug in".
"It's a connectionâ¦ that you can basically use pretty fast, you don't need any special equipment, you don't need to prepare, you just go to the field and usually it works," Neo, a soldier with one of Ukraine's drone reconnaissance units, told the Today programme.
The network has become "the backbone of military communications in Ukraine", George Barros from the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) said, and is used across Kyiv's naval, land, and air forces.
In Ukraine, both Starlink (the civilian service) and Starshield (the military service) are used, depending on what communications are needed.
It is crucial for the effective use of weapons such as drones, which connect to the network so that operators can see their targets in real time.
The technology effectively allows "drones, artillery and command posts to function as a single real-time network where the time between sensor-to-shooter is minimised," Barros, who is the ISW's Director of Innovation and Open Source Tradecraft, told the BBC.
Ukraine also relies on the Starlink network to protect its own skies against incoming Russian attacks, especially jet-powered Shahed drones, Barros said.
Shaheds fly at speeds in excess of 198mph (319 km/h), meaning SpaceX's restriction makes Ukrainian efforts to chase them down all but impossible.
With no ready replacement for the Starlink network, any speed restrictions or loss of connectivity have major implications for Ukraine defences, and the recent limits have shown how dependent Kyiv is on the network.
Image caption, Starlink terminals, like this one in Ukraine's Donetsk region, are quick and easy to set up, making them ideal for use on the battlefield
While Starlink can provide access nearly everywhere in the world, that does not mean it can be accessed everywhere, and countries must be licenced to use it.
Russia is one place where it is not authorised, although Kyiv has in the past said that Moscow was still getting hold of the terminals and using them in occupied territory in Ukraine.
"If SpaceX obtains knowledge that Starlink terminal is being used by a sanctioned or unauthorized party, we investigate the claim and take actions to deactivate the terminal if confirmed," Starlink said in 2024.
But with tens of thousands of terminals in Ukraine alone, it could be a near impossible task to determine which terminals are authorised and which ones are not.

items.title: Are the European Women's World Cup play-offs working?
items.summary: The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
items.content:
Image caption, England have lost just once this year but have still not qualified for the 2027 Women's World Cup
The ease in which England saw off Greece in round one of the Women's World Cup qualifying play-offs showed just how inefficient the structure currently is.
The two-time European champions were superior in every sense as they won 8-1 on aggregate against a Greece side ranked 55 places lower in the world.
Realistically, Greece stood little chance in a two-legged tie against Sarina Wiegman's side despite performing well in their home 3-1 defeat.
England's resounding victory was not a one-off as Europe's other top nations, who were forced to drop into the play-offs, also met lower-ranked opposition and won emphatically.
It was not an evening that truly reflects the growth of European women's football, which has become more competitive than ever in recent years.
It was, however, indicative that the qualification process perhaps needs reviewing by Uefa.
'Unplayable' Stanway a free-scoring warrior for Lionesses
One of the main reasons for Tuesday night's results was that only one team from the league phase groups received automatic qualification.
The Netherlands, 2017 European champions, finished second in their group behind France, ranked sixth in the world. They went on to beat Hungary 11-0 on aggregate.
Norway, World Cup winners in 1995 and six-time European finalists, lost out to giants Germany in their group and ended up beating Romania 8-0.
Other League A fallouts Sweden and the Republic of Ireland thrashed their opponents 15-0 and 12-0 respectively.
So it was no surprise when back-to-back European champions England, who were drawn in the same group as world champions Spain, went on to record another heavy victory against much weaker opposition from League C in their play-off.
"Of course we wanted to qualify straight away, that's not the case," said England manager Wiegman when asked about the qualification process again on Tuesday.
"For us now, the facts are that we are in the play-offs, we have played Greece, now we're through, and now we're going to play Ukraine. That's what my focus is on.
"Uefa will review how things are set up and see whether they think it works or it should be better, or different. I don't think it's my place now to review that."
The Lionesses still have another two-legged tie against Ukraine to play, with the first leg taking place away from home on 1 December and the return fixture at Wembley Stadium on 5 December.
Ukraine are a side who England beat twice in the league phase by an aggregate score of 9-1.
It seems absurd that they should have to beat the same team on at least three occasions as part of their qualification process.
England have won seven of their last eight qualifying matches, scoring 21 goals, conceding just six times, and their only defeat was away from home against world champions Spain.
They came runners-up in League A3 only on their head-to-head record with the best team in the world - they even beat Spain 1-0 at Wembley.
England's overall tally of 15 points in the league phase was beaten by just three other teams - Germany, Switzerland and Hungary.
Switzerland and Hungary were also in qualifying groups in League B and League C that did not include a single team from the world's top 45 ranked nations.
In contrast England, who were seeded in League A, had Iceland - ranked 13th - as a tricky opponent, and world number one Spain in their four-team group.
Image caption, There were several heavy aggregate results in European qualifying
When qualifying for the 2023 Women's World Cup, England beat Latvia on two occasions, winning 20-0 and 10-0 .
That tournament saw an increase from 24 to 32 teams and while qualification was still one-sided, the showpiece in Australia and New Zealand was a different story.
England were tested against debutants Haiti in the group stages, narrowly winning 1-0, and by Colombia in their quarter-final, despite the South American side failing to qualify for the previous tournament.
The level of competition was growing and it was evident even more so across Europe with England failing to qualify for the 2024 Olympic Games on behalf of Team GB after finishing second to the Netherlands in their Nations League group.
A draw with Portugal and defeat by Belgium were suffered by England the following year, while they were forced to overcome two penalty shootouts in Euro 2025.
There is no denying that England's competition has improved but they were still dealt a rough hand in this year's World Cup qualifying campaign.
Following their costly 4-0 defeat by Spain in June, Wiegman said: "The competition in Europe is really high.
"What I'm disappointed about is that we win five games, we have 15 points and we're in a group with the world champions and then you can't qualify.
"I'm happy with the performances but not the result of us having to go into the play-offs. That's just the way it is."
What is frustrating for England is that while they picked up a routine win over Greece and now prepare to face an opponent they have already played twice in 2026, their potential World Cup rivals are getting to play matches against top-tier teams.
Two of the tournament favourites Germany and Japan met in a friendly match on Tuesday night; Brazil and Argentina played out a 2-2 draw and four-time world champions USA played Spain twice in five days in a mouth-watering meeting.
Fifa has announced that the 2031 Women's World Cup will be expanded from 32 to 48 teams and it is too early to know if that is the right decision.
But while larger scorelines remain, it is clear it is more a direct result of a European qualification process that doesn't benefit the majority.

items.summary: Officials meet in Thailand as conflict drives energy prices higher and casts uncertainty over global economy.

The G20 finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering in Bangkok, Thailand [File: Anthony Wallace/AFP]
The G20 finance ministers and central bank governors are gathering in Bangkok, Thailand, on Thursday amid an uncertain global outlook shaped by the US-Israel war on Iran.
The meetings are being held in conjunction with the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, taking place in the Thai capital from October 12 to October 18.

Here are some of the key details about the meetings:
The G20 is an economic forum comprising 19 large economies, including the United States, China, the United Kingdom, Australia, Brazil, India, Japan, Indonesia and Saudi Arabia, as well as the European Union and the African Union.
The grouping has an annually rotating presidency, currently held by the US.
Together, the G20 countries account for about 85 percent of global gross domestic product (GDP) and three-quarters of global trade.
The G20 was established in 1999 as a forum for finance ministers and central bank governors to address shared economic concerns in the wake of the Asian Financial Crisis, before expanding into a broader forum for national leaders.
The IMF, based in Washington, DC, is an international financial institution that promotes international cooperation on monetary policy, trade and economic growth.
Its membership includes all but a handful of the world’s sovereign states, including North Korea, Cuba, the Vatican City and Monaco.
The World Bank, also based in Washington, DC, primarily serves as a provider of loans and grants to developing countries. It has 189 member countries.
The IMF and the World Bank were created at the 1944 Bretton Woods conference in the US, convened by the Allied Powers to establish the contours of the post-World War II international financial order.
Most finance ministers and central bank governors of the G20 will be in Bangkok, along with IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent will be a notable absence from the gatherings, as the top economic official of the world’s biggest economy and G20 chair.
US officials have cited “domestic engagements” for Bessent’s decision to skip the events, at which Washington will be represented by Deputy Secretary Francis Brooke and Undersecretary for International Affairs Erin Browne.
The G20 meeting, one of several gatherings of the group’s finance ministers each year, will help shape the agenda for the headline leaders’ summit in Miami, Florida, taking place on December 14-15.
The economic fallout from the US-Israel war on Iran is expected to dominate discussions.
Attacks across the Middle East have upended economic activity across the region, while disruption to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz has driven a surge in energy prices worldwide.
Crude oil prices have exceeded $100 a barrel for much of the past eight months, placing a strain on government coffers and household budgets, particularly in the Gulf region and the rest of Asia.
In advance of the meeting, Australia’s Treasurer Jim Chalmers MP said he would use the discussions to call for an end to the conflicts in the Middle East and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz “because that’s what the global economy desperately needs”.
“The war in the Middle East is having a devastating economic impact and is pushing up fuel prices, inflation and interest rates around the world,” Chalmers said in a statement.
Other issues likely to feature on the agenda include the ballooning debt levels of many countries, which exceed 100 percent of GDP in the US, Canada, Japan, Italy and France.
In a speech on Wednesday, Georgieva warned that mounting debt posed a threat to the global economy and that there was no “magic” formula that would allow governments to avoid tax hikes or spending cuts.
G20 members will also bring more specific individual concerns to the table based on their economic and geopolitical priorities.
The US, for example, has repeatedly expressed concern about “global imbalances”, a veiled reference to China’s state-driven industrial model that has allowed Chinese exporters to flood overseas markets with cheap goods.
US President Donald Trump has long claimed that China’s large trade surplus, which stood at a cumulative $938bn in September, proves that international trade is stacked against US manufacturers.
In a statement addressed to the IMF on Wednesday, Bessent called for action to address mismatched trade balances.
“This especially includes strengthening its analysis and engagement on the role non-market policies and practices and exchange rates play in driving external imbalances,” Bessent said.
“Policymakers around the world are having difficult discussions about how to sustain market-based systems amid distortionary policies from some economies that skew competition and hurt employment.”
Divisions and competing interests cloud the prospects for coordination, however.
At the last meeting of G20 finance ministers in Asheville, North Carolina, US, held on August 31 and September 1, member countries failed to issue a joint communique after China objected to language to do with trade.

items.title: The Stock Market Is Echoing a Warning From the Dot-Com Bubble, and History Says Investors Should Make This 1 Move - The Motley Fool
items.summary: The Stock Market Is Echoing a Warning From the Dot-Com Bubble, and History Says Investors Should Make This 1 Move  The Motley Fool
items.content:
The S&P 500 has been climbing in recent years, reaching multiple record highs, and the momentum has generally continued in 2026. If we look at the past three calendar years and add in the performance this year so far, the gain totals 100%. And one thing in particular has fueled this movement: investors' excitement about artificial intelligence (AI).
AI, with its potential to transform the way many things are done and supercharge corporate earnings growth, looks like the next big thing in technology -- and a bet in such a space could result in a major win for investors. Many investors have already experienced this victory, considering the double-, triple-, and even quadruple-digit gains of some AI stocks over the past few years. For example, AI chip leader Nvidia has jumped 900% in five years, and memory and storage maker Micron Technology has climbed 200% this year alone.
Since many companies operating in AI are also tech giants that are heavily weighted in the S&P 500, their gains have offered the index a clear direction. Of course, stocks across industries have also advanced, but tech players have played the biggest role.
Against this positive backdrop, however, a storm may be brewing. The stock market is echoing a warning from the dot-com bubble, and history says investors should make one move in particular.
So, first let's dive a little deeper into the current market situation. Investors have been piling into AI stocks in recent years as companies develop the technology, and AI is increasingly being put to use -- though we're in the early days of this phase. As all of that unfolded, certain companies, such as chip designers and cloud companies, began generating significant revenue. Today, with demand for chips and infrastructure high, tech giants must invest heavily to keep pace. For example, Amazon , Microsoft , Alphabet , and Meta Platforms are expected to spend more than $700 billion this year.
Meanwhile, some investors have wondered whether the revenue opportunity will truly justify such spending levels -- and this concern has weighed periodically on the performance of AI stocks. Other headwinds include questions about rising inflation and interest rate levels in the months to come as well as general concerns about the economy and geopolitical environment. All of this has put pressure on stocks on occasion this year, but, overall, the S&P 500 and investors have managed to shake off the worries.
Now, let's consider the storm that's brewing behind the scenes. The stock market is echoing a warning that we saw at a troubling time, during the dot-com bubble... and this is a significant increase in one particular metric. I'm talking about the Buffett indicator, which measures the value of all U.S. publicly listed companies in relation to the country's gross domestic product.
Billionaire investor Warren Buffett introduced this measure in an essay in Fortune back in 2001. "It is probably the best single measure of where valuations stand at any given moment," he wrote.
Today, this indicator delivers an alarming message: It has reached the level of 238%, its highest ever. For reference, it came in at about 148% during the dot-com bubble. So this tells us that stocks are historically expensive today and the underlying economy isn't driving the gains.
What may happen next? A look at history, focusing on the dot-com era back in 2000 and late 2021 when the Buffett indicator soared once again, may offer some answers.
The S&P 500 fell following these peak Buffett indicator readings, and that suggests the stock market today may also be heading for a decline. But before you get too worried about this potential happening, it's important to look a bit farther down the road. And here, we can see that each time, the S&P 500 has always recovered and then gained over a number of years.
History tells us you should make one key move now, and that's to hold onto your positions for the long term. Even if stocks follow historical patterns and decline, the market has proven its ability to deliver a win to investors over the long run. By jumping out of the market, you could incur losses and miss out on gains farther up the path. So, even if the Buffett indicator is flashing a warning signal, the best thing you can do is stay calm and wait for any potential storm to pass.
